content: Streptomycin is associated with an increased risk of ototoxicity (damage to the ear, including hearing loss and balance issues) and nephrotoxicity (damage to the kidneys). Patients receiving this medication should be closely monitored for these adverse effects. Trazodone can reduce the levels or effects of streptomycin by interacting with the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Caution is advised, and monitoring is recommended when these drugs are used together. The combination of streptomycin and trimagnesium citrate anhydrous may enhance the effects of one another, potentially leading to increased toxicity. Caution and close monitoring are necessary. Co-administration of aminoglycosides (like streptomycin) with magnesium can increase the risk of neuromuscular weakness and paralysis. Streptomycin decreases the efficacy of live typhoid vaccine due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. This combination is contraindicated. Streptomycin and vancomycin, when used together, can increase the risk of nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Although the significance of this interaction is uncertain, caution is advised. Streptomycin can enhance the effects of vecuronium through pharmacodynamic synergy, increasing the risk of apnea. This combination should be avoided, or alternative drugs should be considered. Verapamil can increase the levels or effects of streptomycin by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. The combination of voclosporin and streptomycin can increase the nephrotoxic and ototoxic potential of each drug. Therapy should be modified, and close monitoring is essential. Co-administration of drugs associated with nephrotoxicity may elevate the risk of acute or chronic kidney damage. Voriconazole may decrease streptomycin levels through an unknown mechanism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear, but it is considered minor. Streptomycin and zoledronic acid may interact through pharmacodynamic synergy, potentially causing additive hypocalcemia. The clinical significance of this interaction is uncertain. Streptomycin can cause a range of adverse effects, including hypotension, neurotoxicity, drowsiness, headache, drug fever, paresthesia, skin rash, nausea, vomiting, eosinophilia, anemia, arthralgia, weakness, tremor, auditory and vestibular ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and respiratory difficulties. It may also lead to neuromuscular blockade and respiratory paralysis, particularly when administered after anesthesia or muscle relaxants. The parenteral form of streptomycin should only be used in settings where appropriate audiometric and laboratory testing facilities are available. Individuals handling streptomycin should take precautions to avoid skin sensitivity reactions. Intramuscular injections should be administered deep into a large muscle mass to minimize the risk of peripheral nerve damage. Patients with preexisting renal insufficiency require extreme caution when determining the dosage regimen. In severely uremic patients, a single dose may result in prolonged high blood levels, increasing the risk of ototoxicity. Alkalinization of urine may help reduce renal irritation during prolonged therapy. Streptomycin can cross the placental barrier and may cause fetal harm, including ototoxicity. Pregnant patients should be informed of the potential risks to the fetus. Streptomycin is also excreted in breast milk, and its use in nursing mothers requires careful consideration of the risks and benefits. Streptomycin should not be prescribed in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection, as this increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria. Patients should be counseled to complete the full course of therapy as directed, even if they feel better early in the treatment. Skipping doses or stopping treatment prematurely may reduce the effectiveness of the therapy and increase the likelihood of bacterial resistance. Streptomycin is used in combination with other medications to treat active tuberculosis (TB), particularly in cases where other TB drugs are ineffective or the infection is drug-resistant. It belongs to the aminoglycoside class of antibiotics and works by interfering with bacterial protein synthesis. This medication is administered via intramuscular injection, typically once daily at the start of TB treatment. The injection site should be rotated daily to prevent local skin reactions. Dosage is based on the type of infection, patient weight, medical condition, streptomycin blood levels, and response to treatment. Patients should be educated on proper preparation and administration techniques if self-administering at home. The medication should be visually inspected for particles or discoloration before use, and any compromised product should not be used. Streptomycin therapy for TB often lasts nine months or longer. After one to two months of daily administration, the frequency may be reduced to two or three times per week, as directed by the physician. Patients should not discontinue streptomycin or other TB medications without medical advice, as this may worsen the infection or lead to drug resistance. Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, stomach upset, loss of appetite, and injection site reactions such as pain, irritation, or redness. Prolonged or repeated use may result in oral thrush or vaginal yeast infections. Serious allergic reactions are rare but possible. Patients should inform their healthcare provider of any allergies, particularly to aminoglycosides, and provide a complete list of all medications and supplements they are taking to avoid potential drug interactions. Streptomycin may interfere with the efficacy of live bacterial vaccines, such as BCG or typhoid vaccine. In cases of overdose, immediate medical attention is required. Patients should adhere to all scheduled medical and laboratory appointments to monitor kidney function, hearing, and streptomycin blood levels. Unmixed streptomycin should be stored at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Reconstituted solutions are stable for one week at room temperature but should be protected from light. Proper disposal of expired or unused medication is essential.
